newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr too weary to put faith in wage talk.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr too weary to put faith in wage talk.

text.p: Persistent speculative and technical selling knocked the Australian dollar down to fresh 18-month lows Tuesday, a pattern which was threatening to become routine.
The money market was ruffled late in the day when industrial relations minister Peter Reith said some wage claims were too high and "would not be good for interest rates."

Traders said the comments had scant impact on a bearish currency market, where the general reaction was to note that such warnings had been issued many times before but the Reserve Bank had still cut rates four times in the last year.
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the local dollar was wallowing at US$0.7360/65, its fourth successive 18-month closing low, having slipped from US$0.7375/80 late here Monday.
That was just above the intra-day trough of US$0.7348 but still nearly a cent down from Friday's finish of US$0.7445/50 and below important chart support at US$0.7380 and US$0.7410.

Traders said exporter and Asian bank bids were offering temporary assistance but, with US$0.7350 now creaking under the weight of offers, most thought it only a matter of time before last year's US$0.7305 low was revisited. Only a rally back above US$0.7440 would counter the immediate bearish trend, they added.

The area around 73 cents was also an important Fibonacci level being a 50 percent retracement of the entire uptrend from its US$0.6420 trough in October 1993 to the US$0.8210 high seen so briefly in December 1996.

Breaching this would thus be very significant from a technical viewpoint and could entail a further retreat to the next major targets of US$0.7100, which would be a 62 percent retracement of the uptrend, and the 1995 low point of US$0.7070.
Analysts reckoned it would require a break back above the US$0.7650/80 resistance area established in late May/early June to reverse the bear trend -- a rally of three cents from here.
Such a recovery was not beyond the scope of imagination but would require the market to be misplaced in its expectations of another RBA rate cut.

The comments from Reith should, therefore, have been supportive of the dollar on face value. He said some demands for wage rises at the moment would push wages growth above Reserve Bank targets and would not be good for (lower) interest rates.

The RBA has often expressed discomfort at annual wages growth above 4.5-5.0 percent and explicitly linked its last easing on May 23 to a downward revision in earnings growth to below 4.5 percent reported for Q1.
Reith softened the warning somewhat, however, by adding that there had been some relatively benign developments on the wages front over the last 12 months.
This fit the market's bearish mood better with dealers discounting the comments as jawboning for public consumption and of no relevance to monetary policy.

A run of weak jobs data has seen futures market price in a 50 basis point easing in the cash rate to 5.0 percent and most analysts believe the bank is only waiting on confirmation of the extremely benign inflation enviroment from data next week before delivering.

Analysts are confident the quarterly consumer price data will show both headline and underlying inflation falling further and many expect annual growth in the latter to reach 1.7 percent, its lowest level since the series began in the early 1970s.

On the crosses the local currency edged up on the yen to 85.00/10 from 83.70/80 but remains essentially range-bound along with US$/yen. The dollar remained firm on the mark, one of the few major currencies in the world weaker than itself, and was steady at 56.5 in trade weighted terms.
